newsitem.title: CHINA: China foreign bank yuan business growing but capped.
newsitem.headline: China foreign bank yuan business growing but capped.

text.p: Foreign banks handling Chinese yuan are finding business in the newly-opened area is growing steadily but is capped by restrictions that will be around for a while, bankers said on Monday.
"Business has been pretty successful so far," said Tsutomu Hiroe, chief representative of the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd in Shanghai.

Tokyo-Mitsubishi had opened more than 100 local currency accounts and made six yuan loans worth several tens of millions of yuan since winning a licence to do local currency business in April, Hiroe said.
"Volume is not very big but that's because we've just begun and are limited to foreign companies," Hiroe said, adding he hoped to boost the number of accounts to 300-400 within a year.
Other bankers said their business was evolving similarly, with deposits growing in line with expectations but still below the volume needed to really back their yuan loans.
"In terms of amount, it's nothing to brag about," said Ty Tan, chief representative of U.S.-based Citibank. "But at the beginning we made very conservative projections."

To meet the funding shortfall, most banks have been forced to dip into their required $30 million operating capital because interest rates on the interbank market were too high to make money by using the funds to do commercial loans, bankers said.

"The interbank market interest rates are quite high so banks rely on the deposits and the operating capital," said Jethro Lau, general manager of Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp Ltd's Shanghai branch.
"You can't use the interbank market to finance your loans," Citibank's Tan said. "In that scenario, we have to operate on the deposits."
Other bankers said being able to trade on the first tier of China's tightly controlled interbank market was a prime goal of foreign banks in Shanghai.
China has kept tight control of its interbank market by only allowing a "first tier" of state banks and short-term financial centres to directly swap funds on the exchange.
A second tier, which includes foreign banks, must go through the first tier to trade on the market.

Foreign banks also face other official obstacles in their yuan business, ranging from a 30 million yuan cap on interbank transactions to being limited to dealing only with foreign firms based in Shanghai.
Bankers said while they were giving feedback to regulators and would like eventually to see those barriers toppled, the market was still too young to expect liberalisation soon.
"The market has not developed to the degree that you can go and say 'I want to do more'," Tan said.
Dozens of foreign banks have opened branches in Shanghai but regulators have so far allowed only nine to do yuan business, requiring them to move their offices to its Pudong area for the privilege.
Citibank's Tan said he would like to see more foreign banks enter the Shanghai yuan market to boost liquidity.

But Beijing would strive to ensure foreign institutions did not flourish at the expense of China's own fledgling banking sector, which it hopes will someday rival Hong Kong's as a major financial player in Asia.
"You wouldn't need that long of a time for foreign banks to wipe out the local banks," Tan said. "You don't need to be a rocket scientist to figure that out."
